title: Bigheads
blurb: An attempt to smuggle an artwork into a game. Built at Manchester Innovation Lab to test how we can bring a MeYouAndUs approach to a game and also how far we can push what's possible on mobile web. (Pretty much everything you can do in a native app). The central concept is that you scan your head and become the main character in a series of mini games. And also invite your friends to compete with you. We take advantage of all the phone's sensors and cameras to make the controls as tactile and haptic as possible.

title: TILO v2
blurb: The second generation of our hybrid display system for cultural venues, commissioned by Phoenix Leicester. Version two rebuilt the platform on a decade of lessons from the original. We applied the same principle: a public-facing display should allow curators to present an automated playlist of venue information, live data, interactive art, and video content. It was also an opportunity to create some new work and reimagine some older work like When I Grow Up.

title: Fantasia Express
commissioner: Innovate UK - First of a Kind
blurb:
Twelve months of research into location-based augmented reality inside a moving train carriage, funded by Innovate UK's First of a Kind programme with LNER. It ended in a two-week public trial on the East Coast Main Line, turning a carriage full of people looking down into one full of people looking out the window and connecting to the myths and legends in the surrounding countryside.

Actually, that is a lie. The Fantasia Express is an alien spaceship sent to collect relics of our imagination, and what happens when Predator meets The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.
credits: With LNER, Corporation Pop and Immersive Storylab

title: BIGMOUTH
blurb: Participants were asked to speak what they hated about the world into a megaphone whose microphone had been replaced with a camera, which silently projected the words onto a large 360-degree spherical display. They could then look through a small eyepiece on the side of the installation to see their recorded words become the mouth head of a small demon who carried the burden away. A cross between a confessional and Room 101. Also a commentary on censorship and free speech.
credits: Demon illustrations by Tomo. Spherical projection with Pufferfish Displays

title: Cakenocake
blurb: A self-initiated project to explore what a MeYouAndUs project would look like with no technology. Exploring how to corral people into making choices based on which side of a signboard they chose to walk past. Many questions were silly and gradually became more contentious. Being a blackboard allowed us to react to what we saw. For instance, some Jehovah's Witnesses set up quite close and prompted the God or No God question, sending the God people their way.
posterAlt: A chalkboard signboard standing in a busy pedestrian shopping street, TRUMP written on one half and NO TRUMP on the other, with two painted hands in stars-and-stripes sleeves pointing opposite ways. Shoppers walk past on both sides.

title: Emofie
blurb: Everyone was taking selfies, and everyone was sending emojis, so we put one inside the other. Emofie asked you to pull the face yourself. Hold it, and your face became the emoji, then the emoji became a short animation you could keep. Made with Phoenix in Leicester as a phone piece and a gallery installation at the same time.

title: When I Grow Up
blurb: Children picked a future self on an iPad, career, age and appearance, and watched a hand-drawn avatar of it mirror their movements across the cafe video wall. When they left, the avatar stayed behind for the next visitor to wear. Jump, and you swapped into someone else's abandoned future. Made for Phoenix's Sparks children's festival in 2014, and brought back nine years later to launch TILO v2.
posterAlt: A hand holds up a phone running an avatar builder, with tabs for hair, face, eyes and mouth and a DONE button. On the video wall behind, the finished figure stands at full height against a knitted backdrop.

title: TILO
commissioner: Digital R&D Fund for the Arts
blurb: A hybrid display system for arts and cultural venues, funded by the Digital R&D Fund for the Arts. As public realm artists we saw the potential to bring our approach into those public areas. To create screens that could be agile and run interactive artworks alongside the existing programme. We wanted the screens to reflect the whole building's activities. To schedule adverts, data-driven visualisations, artworks and video on a single playlist. We called it TILO as it's the name of a god in some cultures, and we wanted our screens to become the spirit of the buildings they lived in.
posterAlt: Two children stand with their backs to the camera in front of a wall of tiled screens showing a hand-drawn figure in a pink running vest numbered 7. Pink labels across the bottom read information, live data, interactive, personal and art.
credits: With Amaze and Pixel Inspiration. Research by the Creative Exchange, Lancaster University. Music: Luke Howard

title: The Humble Market
blurb: A trading floor for the things that cannot be traded. Lead artists on a collaboration between four Brazilian and UK artists, with a replica Rio taxi, a fake radio station and an Intimatron. It ran as a summer exhibition at FACT, as a performance under a railway arch in Preston for the London 2012 Cultural Olympiad, and at the 2014 World Cup in Belo Horizonte, where the Brazilian Ministry of Culture picked it for the national arts programme. With ZU UK.

title: MeYouAndUs
commissioner: FACT · BBC Big Screens · Robots and Avatars
blurb: One of our simplest yet most effective crowd pleasers, and the artworks that named our practice. It ran on BBC Big Screens in Manchester, Leicester and Edinburgh, in a town square in Miguel Pereira, Brazil, at FACT in Liverpool, and in Robots and Avatars, a European touring exhibition.

title: Not the Beatles Tour
blurb: A prototype for our walking tours platform. An alternative musical tour of Liverpool, as much about where it came from as who made it. It starts in Toxteth in the seventies, home to one of Britain's oldest Black communities and to The Real Thing, whose route to a number one ran through a decade of discrimination, deprivation and hostile policing that ended in the 1981 riots. Then the eighties, where Frankie Goes to Hollywood comes up through the queer scene, and on by decade. Your location decides what plays next. No app store, no headset, no guide with an umbrella.

title: Homewalk
blurb: The first exhibition held at Phoenix post-COVID. After 12 months of the home being everyone's everything. We invited people to come back into the city and bring their home with them. They would take a photo of their front door and then be prompted to take photos that responded to prompts along a curated walk from their home into the centre of Leicester, where an installation would compile everyone's photos onto a giant screen and also allow them to activate an animation of their own photo-walk.
posterAlt: Two hands hold a phone at the kerb of a bus stop. The screen shows a street map with a route traced across it and an orange panel along the bottom.

title: Kindred Spirits
blurb: An evening takeover of Tate Liverpool built from Mondrian, with the Tate Collective and the Costumologists. Visitors chose one of four coloured tickets, each a feeling drawn from Mondrian's writings, then made costumes in those colours and wore them round the exhibition. The tour ended on the fourth floor in a room they had not been told about. Thirty-six screens, thirty-six Raspberry Pis, half a kilometre of cable. Scanning your ticket made you the star of it for a moment, then showed you everyone else who had chosen your colour.
credits: With Tate Collective and the Costumologists. Audio by Kepla

title: Sonic Market
blurb: A lot of data-driven artworks feel like the data abstracted from the representation. Sonic Market installed an industrial weather station on the roof of a working Brighton market, let it control the parameters of a virtual analogue synthesiser, then hung microphones below and fed the market's own sound back into the same machine. Wind and rain arrive as changes you can hear. You might hear an ambulance go past, followed a few seconds later by a jazz ambulance. A permanent installation for Brighton Digital Festival.

title: Invisible Arts Network
blurb: We became artists in residence for Rural Media to lead a six-month project developing a new arts network for Herefordshire that would bring artists, developers and arts organisations together to look at the use of creative technology in contemporary practice. We launched the network (IAN) with a large event, with a lot of help from our friends Mash Cinema, that combined a day conference with a public party in the evening. Called The Happening, it was a celebration of 1960s psychedelia combined with the latest 360 cinema, virtual reality and digital art.
posterAlt: People sit around a table in a whitewashed brick room, seen from behind. Wireless headphones and a small radio transmitter lie on the table, and a jug of wildflowers stands on the shelf behind.

title: Handprint 2012
blurb: An online artwork, a run of live interventions and a mass-participation finale for the North West's Cultural Olympiad. The web piece lived within WE PLAY, the region's London 2012 legacy programme, and drew connections among everyone taking part. It ended over four September nights in Avenham Park, Preston, where two scanning stations and four projectors threw hundreds of freshly scanned hands onto a railway bridge. One surprise was seeing the hands seemingly touch the water, and we created on-site animations to reinforce this perspective, with the hands appearing to come out of the water.
posterAlt: A stone railway viaduct at night with green and blue handprints projected across its arches, one large pale handprint centred in an arch, all reflected in the dark water below.
credits: Part of WE PLAY, the North West's London 2012 legacy programme

title: 26:14:17 (WAITING)
blurb: A permanent installation in the waiting room of a new-build NHS health centre on Townsend Lane, Liverpool. Seventy-two local people were filmed waiting at bus stops on hot summer days. We slowed down the films and, combined with the positivity of a sunny day, created a cinematic view of local people waiting at bus stops for patients in the health centre.
posterAlt: Three vertical panels side by side, each showing a pair of people standing at a bus stop on a sunny street, looking straight at the camera.
credits: Community engagement led by tenantspin with ABCC

title: Wishing Well
blurb: A permanent interactive installation in the courtyard garden of a new-build health centre on Mere Lane, Liverpool. The sister commission to 26:14:17, made through the same programme of community workshops for the Decade of Health and Wellbeing. Taking some of our handprint technology to reimagine a wishing well in a quiet courtyard garden. Creating a contemplative visual record of visitors to the health centre.

title: Lowry to Life
blurb: Two linked installations on opposite sides of the city, built from L.S. Lowry's 1954 painting of Piccadilly Gardens and commissioned to mark the University of Salford's move to MediaCityUK. Each installation reflected a different perspective on the painting, connected telematically across Salford. Lowry's crowds were brought to life by the descendants of the people he painted. Covered by the Guardian and the BBC.

title: Handprint
blurb: For four December evenings, passers-by left giant handprints on City Tower, the 107-metre block in Piccadilly Gardens. Briefly, Manchester's most distinctive canvas. The first Handprint, funded by Arts Council England, made before MeYouAndUs existed as a company and the work everything under that name grew from. The same gesture came back four years later to close the North West's Cultural Olympiad.
